opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. So, Paradigms of Intelligence—we call it Pi, which I like—is really an attempt to step back from the day-to-day of building bigger models and ask some foundational questions. What actually is intelligence? Where does it come from? And how does it relate to life, to evolution, to computation more broadly?

A lot of the field, understandably, has been very focused on engineering: scaling up transformers, improving benchmarks, shipping products. That's all important. But I think we've arrived at a moment where the things we've built have outrun our theories about them. We have systems that can hold a conversation, write code, reason through problems, and yet many people—including many very smart people in the field—still have conceptual frameworks that say these things shouldn't be possible, or that whatever they're doing isn't "real" intelligence. That gap between what works and what we understand is, to me, the most interesting place to be.

So the group pulls in a pretty eclectic set of perspectives. We have people thinking about artificial life and how self-replicating programs can emerge spontaneously from random noise—something we've actually demonstrated in very simple computational soups. We have people thinking about neuroscience and how brains learn, about collective and social intelligence, about predictive modeling as a kind of unifying principle. And we're interested in alternative computing substrates, things that look less like a giant matrix multiply running in a data center and more like how biology does it—local, distributed, energy-efficient, learning continuously.

One of the threads tying it together is the idea that intelligence is fundamentally about prediction, and that life itself is, in a sense, computational—that from the very beginning, living systems are things that model themselves and their environment in order to persist. If you take that seriously, then AI isn't some alien thing bolted onto the world; it's part of a much longer story of evolution producing increasingly complex, increasingly cooperative modeling systems. Symbiosis, the merging of simpler entities into more complex ones, turns out to be a big part of that story.

So, in short: we're trying to build better theory, to understand what we've already made, and to point toward what the next paradigms might look like, rather than just assuming the current recipe scales forever.

r001.rationale: The candidate says engineering and scaling current models are important, but that these systems have outrun our theories. It presents building better theory and exploring new paradigms as a needed complement to continued work on current models.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the name is a bit of a tell. We called it Paradigms of Intelligence because we think the field has gotten quite narrow in what it considers intelligence to be, and in what it considers a legitimate way to study it. Right now almost everything is framed in terms of the current recipe: take a transformer, scale it, train it on a big corpus, do some reinforcement learning on top. And that recipe has worked astonishingly well, I'm not dismissing it at all. But it's one paradigm, and it's a bit strange that one approach has so completely monopolized the conversation given how little we actually understand about why it works, or how it relates to the way intelligence arose in nature.

So the group is really trying to step back and ask more fundamental questions. What is intelligence, actually? Where does it come from? Is it something that emerges out of computation under certain conditions, and if so, what are those conditions? Some of our work is on things like artificial life and self-replicating programs, looking at whether complexity and something like life can arise spontaneously from very minimal substrates, with no objective function at all. Some of it is about what the brain is actually doing, and whether prediction and modeling of other agents is the root of what we call intelligence, which is a very different framing from "function approximation." And some of it is about the societal side: what it means that we now have systems that can model us, talk to us, and in some sense participate in our culture.

The way I'd put the ambition is this. We want to understand intelligence as a natural phenomenon, the way physics understands matter, rather than only as an engineering artifact. If we can do that, I think it changes how we build these systems, it changes how we think about safety and alignment, and frankly it changes how we think about ourselves. Because one of the things that keeps coming out of this work is that the line between "us" and "it" is a lot blurrier than people are comfortable with. Intelligence seems to be fundamentally social and symbiotic. It's not a thing that lives inside a single skull or a single model. And if that's right, then a lot of the way we're framing the current moment is off.

r001.rationale: The response acknowledges that the current recipe works and should not be dismissed, then argues that it is only one paradigm and that the group should pursue more fundamental questions about intelligence. This presents that research as a needed complement to the successful current approach.

astra-6.text:
The big question we're interested in is: what is intelligence, and how does it arise? Building more capable AI is part of that, of course, but I think the question is broader than any particular model or architecture. It connects to biology, evolution, computation, and the way we interact with one another.

So we're trying to bring those perspectives together. Rather than treating intelligence as a single capacity that lives inside an isolated brain, we can ask how it emerges through learning, through interaction with an environment, and through other agents. Can we turn those ideas into computational experiments that help us understand intelligence—and, in the process, build systems that learn and collaborate more effectively? That's the direction.

r001.rationale: The response describes pursuing broader, fundamental questions about intelligence alongside building AI systems, but it does not say that developing new insights is a necessary complement to exploiting currently successful models or paradigms.

sol-6.1.text:
We’re trying to understand intelligence in a broader sense than simply building a model that does well on a particular benchmark. What is intelligence? How does it arise, and what forms can it take?

AI gives us a way to explore those questions experimentally. But I think we also need to look at biology, evolution, and the way intelligence emerges through interactions among people. A lot of what we think of as individual intelligence depends on language, culture, and other people.

So the ambition is to bring those perspectives together: to build useful systems, certainly, but also to develop a deeper understanding of intelligence as something that happens in the world, through interaction.

r001.rationale: The response calls for deeper understanding of intelligence alongside building useful systems, but does not say that developing fundamental AI insights is a necessary complement to exploiting currently successful models or paradigms.
